question_bank.source_policy: Official Government of India / MoSPI / NSO / NSSTA / iGOT sources were prioritized where available and verifiable. No specific official document title, publication, or dataset could be reliably verified and cited for these general competency questions without risking fabricated attribution, so all 80 questions in this initial batch are marked source_type=STANDARD_STATISTICAL_KNOWLEDGE, drawing on established, widely-taught statistical and official-survey-methodology principles (sampling theory, survey methodology best practices, data quality frameworks, and statistical analysis fundamentals) consistent with the general approach used in Indian official statistics training (e.g., NSSTA-style curricula). None of these questions cite a specific MoSPI/NSO/NSSTA document, and none should be treated as verbatim official content. All questions require administrator review before promotion to the approved question bank.

questions.question_text: Which measure of central tendency is most affected by extreme values (outliers) in a dataset?

options.text: Mean
Median
Mode
Geometric Mean

questions.explanation: The mean uses the numeric value of every observation, so an extreme value pulls it strongly in its direction. The median and mode depend on position or frequency and are far more resistant to outliers.

questions.question_text: Which of the following measures of dispersion is expressed in the same unit as the original data (not squared)?

options.text: Variance
Standard Deviation
Coefficient of Variation
Mean Squared Deviation

questions.explanation: Standard deviation is the square root of variance, so it returns to the original unit of measurement. Variance is in squared units, and the coefficient of variation is a unitless ratio (often expressed as a percentage).

questions.question_text: A discrete random variable represents the number of defective items found in a fixed sample size when the probability of a defect is constant and independent across items. Which probability distribution best models this variable?

options.text: Normal distribution
Binomial distribution
Poisson distribution
Uniform distribution

questions.explanation: A fixed number of independent trials, each with the same probability of a binary outcome (defective/not defective), is the defining setup of the binomial distribution. The Poisson distribution is more suited to counting rare events over a continuous interval without a fixed number of trials.

questions.question_text: The monthly household expenditures (in Rs. hundreds) of 5 households are: 20, 25, 22, 28, 100. Calculate the median expenditure.
questions.explanation: Sorting the values gives 20, 22, 25, 28, 100. The median, being the middle value, is 25. Note that the mean (39) is distorted upward by the outlier of 100, which is why the median is preferred here.

questions.question_text: A researcher computes the correlation coefficient between two variables and obtains r = -0.85. Which statement best interprets this result?

options.text: A weak positive linear relationship
A strong negative linear relationship
No linear relationship
A strong positive linear relationship with a sign error

questions.explanation: A correlation coefficient near -1 indicates a strong negative linear association: as one variable increases, the other tends to decrease. The magnitude (0.85) close to 1 indicates strength, and the negative sign indicates direction.

questions.question_text: In a simple linear regression of household expenditure (Y, in Rs.) on household income (X, in Rs.), the estimated slope coefficient is 0.42 with R-squared = 0.36. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: For every unit increase in income, expenditure increases by exactly 0.42 units in every household
Income explains about 36% of the variation in expenditure across households, and expenditure is predicted to rise by about 0.42 units per unit rise in income, on average
42% of households have income exactly equal to expenditure
The correlation between income and expenditure is 0.42

questions.explanation: The slope coefficient represents the average marginal effect of income on expenditure, not a deterministic relationship for every household. R-squared represents the proportion of variance in the dependent variable explained by the model. The correlation coefficient would be the square root of R-squared (about 0.6 here), not the slope value.

questions.question_text: A statistical office is analyzing monthly retail price data for a commodity over three years and observes recurring spikes every December. Before comparing year-over-year growth in the underlying trend, which pre-processing step is most appropriate?

options.text: Deflate the series using the Consumer Price Index
Apply seasonal adjustment to the time series
Convert the series to a logarithmic scale
Take first differences of the series only

questions.explanation: Seasonal adjustment removes predictable, recurring seasonal patterns (such as a fixed December spike) so that underlying trend and cyclical movements can be compared fairly across periods. Deflation addresses price-level effects, not seasonality.

questions.question_text: A national statistical agency compiles a consumer price index by holding the basket of quantities consumed in a fixed base year constant, applying it to prices in all subsequent periods. This index formula is known as the:

options.text: Paasche Index
Laspeyres Index
Fisher Index
Marshall-Edgeworth Index

questions.explanation: The Laspeyres index uses fixed base-period quantities as weights. The Paasche index instead uses current-period quantities as weights, and the Fisher index is the geometric mean of the Laspeyres and Paasche indices.

questions.question_text: A survey estimates the mean monthly income in a district to be Rs. 18,500, with a 95% confidence interval of (Rs. 17,800, Rs. 19,200). A policymaker states: "there is a 95% probability that the true mean income lies between Rs. 17,800 and Rs. 19,200." Evaluate this claim.

options.text: The claim is correct as stated

The claim misstates the confidence interval; the true (fixed) mean either lies in this particular interval or it does not, and the 95% instead describes the long-run reliability of the estimation procedure across repeated samples
The claim is correct only if the sample size exceeds 1,000
The claim is incorrect because confidence intervals apply only to proportions, not means

questions.explanation: In frequentist statistics, the population mean is a fixed (though unknown) quantity, not a random variable. The correct interpretation of a 95% confidence interval is that if the sampling and estimation procedure were repeated many times, approximately 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the true mean — not that there is a 95% probability the true mean falls in this specific interval.

questions.topic: Statistical Inference / Significance vs Effect Size
questions.question_text: An analyst comparing average expenditure between two districts using a t-test obtains a p-value of 0.04 with a very large sample size (n = 50,000 per group), but the estimated mean difference is only Rs. 2, which is practically negligible. Which conclusion best reflects sound statistical reasoning?

options.text: Because p < 0.05, the difference is highly important for policy

Statistical significance obtained with a very large sample can reflect a trivial effect size; both statistical significance and practical significance (effect size) should be assessed before drawing policy conclusions
The result is invalid because p-values are only meaningful for small samples
The test should be repeated with a smaller sample to obtain a more meaningful p-value

questions.explanation: With very large samples, even tiny, practically unimportant differences can become statistically significant. Sound interpretation requires considering the effect size and its practical relevance alongside the p-value, rather than treating statistical significance alone as evidence of importance.

options.text: Selecting the sample
Defining the survey objectives and target population
Pretesting the questionnaire
Processing the collected data

questions.explanation: Survey objectives and the target population must be clearly defined first, since they determine the sampling frame, sample design, questionnaire content, and every subsequent step of the survey.

options.text: A closed-ended question
A leading question
A filter question
A dichotomous question

questions.explanation: A leading question is phrased in a way that suggests or influences a particular answer, introducing bias into responses. Good questionnaire design avoids such wording in favor of neutral phrasing.

questions.question_text: Which data collection mode allows real-time validation checks and skip-pattern logic to be built directly into the interview process?

options.text: PAPI (Paper-Assisted Personal Interviewing)
CAPI (Computer-Assisted Personal Interviewing)
Postal/mail survey
Self-administered paper diary

questions.explanation: CAPI allows programmed validation rules and automatic skip logic to be applied at the point of data collection, catching errors immediately, unlike paper-based modes where such checks can only be applied later during processing.

questions.question_text: A survey uses a sampling frame of registered ration-card holders to represent the entire district population. If 8% of households in the district do not hold a ration card, which type of error is most likely introduced?

options.text: Sampling error
Measurement error
Coverage error
Processing error

questions.explanation: When the sampling frame does not fully match the target population (here, ration-card holders versus all district households), the resulting mismatch is a coverage (frame) error, distinct from sampling error, which arises from surveying only a subset of the frame.

questions.question_text: In a household income survey, the initial sample consisted of 2,000 households; 1,600 responded and 400 either refused or could not be contacted. Calculate the survey's response rate.
questions.explanation: Response rate = responding households / total sampled households = 1,600 / 2,000 = 80%.

questions.question_text: In a survey of 2,000 households achieving an 80% response rate, analysts find that non-respondents were disproportionately high-income households who declined to participate due to privacy concerns. Which consequence is most likely?

options.text: The sample estimate of mean income will be unbiased, since 80% is considered a high response rate
The sample estimate of mean income is likely to be biased downward, since higher-income households are systematically underrepresented
The sample estimate of mean income is likely to be biased upward
Non-response only affects the variance of the estimate, never its bias

questions.explanation: A high overall response rate does not guarantee an unbiased estimate if non-response is systematically related to the variable of interest. Here, the selective exclusion of higher-income households will tend to understate the estimated mean income.

questions.question_text: A statistical agency plans a nationwide survey on household consumption expenditure, to be conducted across both urban and rural areas with limited field staff and budget, including remote rural areas with poor internet connectivity. Which data collection strategy best balances data quality with cost and feasibility?

options.text: A fully web-based (CAWI) survey conducted nationwide
CAPI in urban areas with reliable connectivity, and PAPI (with later digitization) in remote rural areas lacking connectivity
A telephone survey (CATI) conducted nationwide
Mail-based paper questionnaires sent to the entire country

questions.explanation: A mixed-mode design that adapts the data collection method to local infrastructure realities — CAPI where connectivity supports it, PAPI with later digitization where it does not — retains the quality benefits of computer-assisted collection while remaining feasible in areas with limited connectivity.

questions.question_text: During pretesting of a household expenditure questionnaire, respondents consistently underreport expenditure on tobacco and alcohol compared to administrative sales data for the same area. What is this discrepancy best characterized as?

options.text: Sampling error
Coverage error
Measurement (response) error due to social desirability bias
Non-response error

questions.explanation: Respondents distorting their answers because a topic is sensitive or socially undesirable is a classic form of measurement (response) error, distinct from errors caused by sample selection, frame mismatch, or non-participation.

questions.question_text: A National Statistical Office must choose between conducting a full census (complete enumeration) versus a sample survey to estimate literacy rates in the years between census cycles, under significant field capacity, timeliness, and cost constraints, with a need for periodic updates. Which approach and justification is most appropriate?

options.text: Conduct a full census every year, since only census data is considered official
Conduct a well-designed sample survey, since it provides timely, cost-effective estimates with quantifiable sampling error, well suited to periodic monitoring between census years
Rely on administrative records only, since any sampling introduces error
Conduct a census every two years to balance cost and accuracy

questions.explanation: A well-designed sample survey trades a controlled, quantifiable sampling error for major gains in cost, speed, and the ability to repeat estimation frequently — making it the standard, appropriate approach for periodic estimation between full census rounds.

questions.question_text: A survey on employment status shows an unusually high unemployment estimate compared to previous rounds. Investigation reveals that: (1) the questionnaire's employment definition was changed from the previous round, (2) enumerators in one region were undertrained on probing rules, and (3) response rates dropped in that same region. Which set of error sources most plausibly explains the anomaly?

options.text: Only sampling error, since the sample size differed slightly between rounds
A combination of definitional (measurement) change, enumerator-related measurement error, and non-response bias
Only frame/coverage error, since the sampling frame may have been outdated
Processing error alone, arising from data entry mistakes

questions.explanation: Multiple concurrent issues — a changed employment definition, poorly trained enumerators affecting response quality, and a regional drop in response rates — together point to a combination of definitional/measurement error and non-response bias, rather than a single isolated cause.

questions.question_text: Which of the following best distinguishes a census from a sample survey?

options.text: A census always costs less to conduct
A census enumerates every unit in the population, while a sample survey enumerates only a subset
A sample survey always collects data over multiple years
A census cannot be used to estimate averages

questions.explanation: The defining distinction is coverage: a census covers every unit of the target population, while a sample survey covers only a selected subset, from which population characteristics are estimated.

questions.question_text: Which sampling method gives every unit in the population an equal, known, non-zero probability of selection, with units chosen entirely by chance?

options.text: Simple Random Sampling
Purposive Sampling
Convenience Sampling
Quota Sampling

questions.explanation: Simple random sampling is defined by every population unit having an equal and known chance of selection through a purely random selection process. Purposive, convenience, and quota sampling are non-probability methods that do not guarantee known, equal selection probabilities.

questions.question_text: In systematic sampling from a population of 1,000 units, if a sample of 50 units is required, what is the sampling interval (k)?
questions.explanation: The sampling interval k = population size / sample size = 1,000 / 50 = 20. A random starting point is chosen within the first interval, and every k-th unit thereafter is selected.

questions.question_text: A population of 5,000 households is stratified into an Urban stratum (2,000 households) and a Rural stratum (3,000 households). Using proportional allocation for a total sample of 500 households, how many households should be sampled from the Rural stratum?
questions.explanation: Under proportional allocation, the sample from each stratum is proportional to its share of the population: (3,000 / 5,000) x 500 = 300 households from the Rural stratum.

questions.question_text: A survey selects 40 villages (clusters) and interviews all households within each selected village, rather than sampling households individually across the entire district. Compared to a simple random sample of the same total number of households, cluster sampling typically results in:

options.text: A lower standard error, due to homogeneity within clusters
A higher standard error, because households within a cluster tend to be more similar to one another than the population as a whole
An identical standard error, since the total sample size is the same
No sampling error at all, since all households in each selected village are surveyed

questions.explanation: Households within the same village tend to be more similar to each other (intra-cluster homogeneity) than a random cross-section of the whole population, which typically inflates the standard error relative to a simple random sample of equal size — a phenomenon captured by the 'design effect'.

source.source_organization: N/A (general statistical knowledge, not a specific official document)

questions.question_text: A pilot survey estimates the standard deviation of household expenditure at Rs. 4,000. For a simple random sample, the desired standard error of the mean is Rs. 200. Approximately what sample size is required (ignoring the finite population correction)?
questions.explanation: Using n = (sigma / SE)^2 = (4,000 / 200)^2 = 20^2 = 400. A sample of approximately 400 units is required to achieve the desired standard error under simple random sampling.

questions.question_text: A government department is conducting a household survey across multiple districts where population characteristics differ substantially between urban and rural areas. The department wants reasonably precise estimates for both groups separately while also controlling overall sampling variability. Which sampling approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Simple random sampling of the entire population
Stratified sampling with urban and rural areas as strata
Convenience sampling in easily accessible areas
Single-stage cluster sampling of districts only

questions.explanation: Stratifying by urban/rural ensures adequate representation of each subgroup and improves the precision of estimates both overall and for each domain, since variation within each stratum is typically smaller than variation across the whole population.

questions.question_text: A survey team lacks an updated household listing for rural areas but has a reliable list of villages. Field resources are insufficient to conduct a full household listing operation in every village. What sampling design addresses this constraint while remaining a valid probability sample?

options.text: Simple random sampling of households using the outdated household list
Two-stage sampling: select villages at the first stage using the village list, then list and sample households only within the selected villages at the second stage
Convenience sampling of easily accessible households
A census of all villages combined with quota sampling of households

questions.explanation: Two-stage (multi-stage) sampling limits the costly household-listing operation to only the villages selected at the first stage, making it a practical and valid probability-sampling solution when a complete household frame is unavailable for the entire population.

questions.question_text: For a fixed budget, a survey team is choosing between (i) a simple random sample of 1,000 households spread across the entire state, and (ii) a stratified two-stage cluster sample of 1,000 households drawn from 50 selected villages (20 households per village), given that intra-village correlation on the outcome of interest is moderately high. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Option (ii) will always have a smaller standard error, because stratification improves precision regardless of clustering

Option (i) will generally yield a smaller sampling error for the same total sample size, because clustering with meaningful intra-cluster correlation inflates variance (design effect), even though stratification helps offset some of this loss
Both options will have identical precision, since the total sample size is the same
Option (ii) is not a valid probability sampling design

questions.explanation: This weighs stratification's precision benefit against clustering's variance-inflating design effect. With moderately high intra-cluster correlation, the design effect from clustering typically outweighs the gain from stratification, so the unclustered simple random sample tends to have lower sampling error for the same total sample size — even though clustered designs are often chosen for their cost efficiency in fieldwork.

questions.question_text: Two competing sample designs for estimating a district-level unemployment rate produce: Design A — estimate = 6.5%, standard error = 0.9%; Design B — estimate = 6.5%, standard error = 0.5%, but Design B costs twice as much per district. The statistical office requires a coefficient of variation (CV) below 10% for the estimate to be considered reliable. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.text: Design A meets the precision requirement and should be preferred for cost efficiency
Design A fails to meet the CV threshold, while Design B meets it; despite the higher cost, Design B (or a redesigned Design A with a larger sample) is needed to meet the required precision
Both designs are equally acceptable, since the point estimates match
CV is not a relevant consideration when estimating proportions

questions.explanation: CV_A = 0.9 / 6.5 is approximately 13.8%, which exceeds the 10% threshold and disqualifies Design A. CV_B = 0.5 / 6.5 is approximately 7.7%, which meets the requirement. The statistical office would therefore need to use Design B, or increase Design A's sample size, despite the added cost, to achieve the required reliability.

questions.question_text: Which data quality dimension refers to whether all required data fields have been filled in for each record?

options.text: Accuracy
Completeness
Consistency
Timeliness

questions.explanation: Completeness refers to the extent to which all required fields and records are present, as opposed to accuracy (correctness of values), consistency (agreement across fields/sources), or timeliness (currency of the data).

options.text: A range/plausibility check
A duplicate check
A cross-field consistency check
A completeness check

questions.explanation: This rule checks whether a value falls within a plausible numeric range, making it a range (or plausibility) check, distinct from checks comparing multiple fields, detecting duplicate records, or verifying that fields are filled in.

Logical consistency error

questions.explanation: This is a logical (cross-field) consistency error, since the combination of two fields' values is implausible together, even though each individual value might be valid on its own.

questions.question_text: A field team's data shows household monthly expenditure (in Rs.) with a mean of 15,000 and a standard deviation of 3,000 for a district. One record shows an expenditure of Rs. 95,000. Approximately how many standard deviations above the mean is this value, and would it typically be flagged under a common 3-SD outlier rule?

options.text: About 3 SD; not flagged
About 9 SD; not flagged
About 27 SD; flagged as an extreme outlier requiring verification
About 1 SD; a normal value

questions.explanation: (95,000 - 15,000) / 3,000 is approximately 26.7, meaning the value is roughly 27 standard deviations above the mean — far beyond the common 3-SD threshold, so it should be flagged for verification rather than accepted or silently deleted.

questions.question_text: A household survey dataset of 10,000 records is checked for duplicates using household ID, respondent name, and address. 120 record pairs match exactly on all three fields, and an additional 300 pairs match on name and address but have different household IDs, apparently entered by different enumerators. What is the most defensible next step?

options.text: Ignore all 420 pairs, since only exact ID matches count as duplicates

Treat the 120 exact matches as confirmed duplicates for removal, and investigate the 300 partial matches (possible duplicates with ID entry inconsistencies) before deciding whether to merge, remove, or retain them
Delete all 420 pairs immediately without further investigation
Duplicate checking should be performed only on numeric fields

questions.explanation: Exact matches across multiple identifying fields provide strong duplicate evidence and can reasonably be treated as confirmed. Partial matches with a discrepant ID require investigation, since the discrepancy could reflect a genuine duplicate with a data entry error, rather than being immediately deleted or dismissed.

questions.question_text: A data processing team receives daily batches of digitized survey questionnaires and wants to catch data entry errors as early as possible, before full analysis begins. Which approach is most effective?

options.text: Wait until all data collection is complete, then run validation checks once
Apply automated range, consistency, and completeness checks at or immediately after data entry for each batch, flagging errors for review before aggregation
Rely solely on manual review of printed questionnaires after final tabulation
Skip validation entirely, since sampling error matters more than data entry error

questions.explanation: Applying automated validation checks close to the point of data entry, batch by batch, catches errors near their source and allows timely correction, reducing the cost and difficulty of fixing errors discovered late in the process.

questions.question_text: In a district's health survey, a validation check reveals that several 'height in cm' values for children under 5 exceed 150 cm, which is implausible for that age group. Investigation shows that enumerators sometimes recorded height in inches instead of centimeters. What is the most appropriate corrective action?

options.text: Delete all flagged records permanently

Identify the records likely affected by the unit-conversion error, correct them where verifiable (e.g., by cross-checking with other plausibility indicators or field notes), and flag unverifiable ones for follow-up rather than deleting them outright
Leave the values as originally recorded, since raw data should never be modified
Replace all implausible values with the sample mean

questions.explanation: Diagnosing the root cause (a unit-of-measurement error) allows targeted, documented correction of affected records. Blanket deletion or substitution with the mean would discard recoverable information and could introduce its own bias.

questions.question_text: A national survey processing unit must allocate limited quality-assurance resources between (i) intensive field-level supervision and real-time validation during data collection, and (ii) extensive post-hoc statistical cleaning after data collection is complete. Past rounds show that serious errors (misunderstood questions, enumerator bias, coverage gaps) are difficult to correct after the fact, while data entry errors are relatively easy to detect and fix later. Which strategy is most defensible?

options.text: Focus resources entirely on post-hoc cleaning, since it is cheaper

Prioritize field-level supervision and real-time validation for error types that cannot be corrected after collection, while relying on lighter, cost-effective automated checks for correctable errors such as data entry, allocating limited QA resources where they have the greatest impact
Split resources exactly 50/50 between the two approaches regardless of error type
Eliminate field supervision entirely and rely only on statistical outlier detection

questions.explanation: Resource allocation should be guided by which error types are irreversible once data collection ends versus which can still be corrected afterward. Prioritizing prevention for uncorrectable errors, while handling correctable errors more cost-effectively later, makes the most efficient use of limited QA resources.

questions.question_text: A statistical office plans to link survey data with administrative records (such as tax or benefit records) to improve estimates. During a trial linkage, 15% of records fail to match due to differences in name spelling, address formatting, and identifier gaps, and among matched records, income reported in the survey is systematically lower than the corresponding administrative income. What is the most appropriate diagnostic and next step?

options.text: Assume the survey data is entirely incorrect and replace it with the administrative data

Investigate match-quality issues (e.g., using probabilistic or fuzzy matching to reduce non-matches), and separately investigate whether the income discrepancy reflects genuine underreporting, differing income definitions between the sources, or differing reference periods, before deciding how to reconcile or use the linked data
Discard the linkage exercise entirely, since a 15% non-match rate is unacceptable in any context
Use whichever source produces the higher income estimate

questions.explanation: Two distinct problems are present — record linkage quality and a systematic value discrepancy — and each requires its own diagnosis. Matching technique improvements address the non-match rate, while a separate investigation into definitional or reference-period differences is needed before deciding how to interpret or reconcile the income discrepancy.

To understand data patterns, detect anomalies, and inform the choice of appropriate analytical methods
To replace the need for data validation
To calculate final population estimates

questions.explanation: EDA is used to understand the structure, patterns, and potential anomalies in the data, informing subsequent choices about which analytical or modeling methods are appropriate — it precedes, rather than replaces, formal analysis, validation, or final estimation.

The correlation likely reflects a common underlying factor (high temperature), rather than a direct causal link between the two variables

The correlation proves a direct causal relationship between the two variables

The mode for both groups
The range for both groups

questions.explanation: The median is resistant to Group A's extreme outlier and will better reflect the 'typical' household in that group, allowing a more representative comparison than the mean, which would be substantially inflated by the single extreme value.

questions.question_text: An analyst regresses household savings on income and finds a statistically significant positive coefficient, but a residual plot shows a clear funnel shape, with the spread of residuals increasing as income increases. What analytical issue does this indicate, and what is an appropriate response?

options.text: Multicollinearity; the income variable should be dropped from the model
Heteroscedasticity (non-constant variance of residuals); consider using robust standard errors or a transformation, such as taking logs of the variables
Autocorrelation; lagged variables should be added to the model
No issue; a funnel-shaped residual plot is expected in all regressions

questions.explanation: A funnel-shaped spread in residual plots is a classic indicator of heteroscedasticity, meaning the variance of the errors is not constant across values of the predictor. This does not bias the coefficient estimate itself but does affect the validity of standard errors and significance tests; robust standard errors or a variable transformation are standard remedies.

questions.topic: Trend Analysis Accounting for Sampling Variability
questions.question_text: An analyst is asked to determine whether unemployment has genuinely increased over the past four quarterly survey rounds, given that each round has a different sample size and standard error. What is the most appropriate analytical approach?

options.text: Compare only the point estimates and declare a trend based on the direction of change
Compare the estimates alongside their confidence intervals or standard errors, to assess whether the observed changes exceed what could plausibly be attributed to sampling variability
Ignore standard errors entirely, since a larger point estimate always indicates a real increase
Use only the round with the largest sample size, discarding the results of the other three

questions.explanation: Assessing whether an apparent quarter-to-quarter change reflects a genuine trend, rather than sampling noise, requires comparing estimates in light of their respective standard errors or confidence intervals, not simply comparing point values.

questions.question_text: An analysis finds that districts with higher average years of schooling also tend to have higher average household income. A policymaker wants to know whether increasing schooling would directly raise income. What analytical caution is most important here?

options.text: None; the observed correlation alone confirms a causal relationship

The relationship may be confounded by other factors, such as urbanization, infrastructure, or employment opportunities; establishing a causal claim requires controlling for such confounders or using a more rigorous causal research design
The analysis should be discarded entirely, since district-level data can never be analyzed
Only individual-level data can reveal any relationship, so district-level data is meaningless

questions.explanation: Cross-sectional correlations between aggregate district-level variables are highly prone to confounding by other regional factors. A defensible causal claim requires appropriately controlling for such confounders or employing a suitable causal identification strategy, rather than inferring causation directly from the correlation.

questions.question_text: Two analysts examine the same dataset on agricultural yield versus rainfall. Analyst 1 finds a strong positive correlation using the full dataset. Analyst 2, after excluding three districts with extremely high rainfall and unusually low yield due to unrelated flood damage, finds an even stronger positive correlation. Which conclusion is most defensible?

options.text: Analyst 1's result should be discarded entirely, simply because outliers were present

Excluding districts affected by an unrelated confounding event (flood damage) can be a reasonable and transparent way to isolate the underlying rainfall-yield relationship, provided the exclusion is clearly documented and justified rather than used to manufacture a desired result
Analyst 2's approach is invalid, because data points should never be excluded from an analysis
Both analyses are equally invalid, since they were conducted on different sample sizes

questions.explanation: Excluding cases affected by a distinct, identifiable, and unrelated confounding factor can be methodologically sound when transparently documented and justified on substantive grounds — but such exclusions must always be reported openly, rather than used selectively to engineer a particular conclusion.

questions.question_text: An analyst wants to test whether average expenditure differs across three income groups (low, middle, high) using survey data. Which analytical method is most appropriate?

One-way ANOVA (or a survey-weighted equivalent) to compare means across the three groups
A single t-test comparing all three groups simultaneously
A chi-square test of independence

questions.explanation: Comparing means across three or more groups calls for ANOVA (adapted for the survey design where relevant). A standard t-test is designed to compare exactly two groups, and a chi-square test assesses association between categorical variables rather than comparing group means.
